title: Foundation or Formula? TimesFM-3 versus classical time-series models — pre-registered protocol, simulation engine, per-series results and manuscript source
description:
The complete research compendium for Foundation or Formula? A Simulation-Based Comparison of Google's TimesFM-3 and Classical Time-Series Models.

Public forecasting benchmarks cannot settle whether a time-series foundation model beats ARIMA, because only about 6% of the 401 datasets used across 22 published foundation models had never appeared in some model's pre-training corpus. This study generates its own data instead. Under a known data-generating process two things hold at once that never hold on a public benchmark: the foundation model provably has not seen the series, and the classical model is correctly specified by construction.

Across 7,200 simulated series (nine processes × four lengths × 200 replications × six methods) plus 2,932 rolling-origin windows over 1,000 M4 Monthly series, neither family dominates. TimesFM-3 wins 16 of 36 cells to the classical methods' 20 — but those 20 are split across five different winners, while TimesFM-3 is a single untuned model that is never worse than 1.31× the best method in any cell, where every classical method is somewhere at least 2.2× worse. The transferable finding is that the decisive property is not whether a classical model is correctly specified but whether it is estimable: given two seasonal cycles, AutoETS lost to the seasonal naive rule by a factor of 2.7 on data an ETS process had itself generated.

This deposit contains everything needed to reproduce every number in the paper:

  • PREREGISTRATION.md — the protocol, including the five hypotheses, frozen before any forecast was produced and never edited afterwards. Two hypotheses were refuted outright and none survived unqualified; all are reported as such.
  • DEVIATIONS.md — every departure from that protocol, dated and reasoned, split into those made before results existed and those made after, including a row-alignment bug that was caught only because seasonal naive returned an impossible value, and an invalid Diebold–Mariano statistic that was deleted rather than reported with a caveat.
  • code/ — the whole pipeline in execution order: nine data-generating processes with a deterministic seeding contract, the metric implementations, the three-phase forecast runner, the pre-registered tests with Benjamini–Hochberg control, the operational benchmark, the M4 tier, the Croston-family supplement, and the checking scripts that validate every DOI and every headline number.
  • results/ — per-series metrics for all 129,600 evaluations, the raw forecasts and quantiles as compressed arrays, and every aggregated table behind the manuscript.
  • figures/ — all figures as vector PDF.
  • manuscript/ — the LaTeX source, the bibliography with every identifier resolved, and the generated tables.

The raw M4 competition archive is not redistributed; the code re-fetches it, and the seeded 1,000-series sample used here is included so the real-data tier reproduces exactly. Code is MIT-licensed; deposited results and figures are CC-BY-4.0.

Note on the model. TimesFM-3's pre-trained weights are released by Google under a non-commercial, non-production licence and are not redistributed here; the code downloads them from Hugging Face.

Version 1.1.0 (September 2026). Revision for the Journal of Forecasting (manuscript in manuscript_jof/, Wiley USG class). All additions are post hoc and logged in DEVIATIONS.md (D-10 to D-12): a representativeness analysis in a feature-based instance space against M4 Monthly; a robustness study with randomised parameters, heavy-tailed noise, outliers and an estimated seasonal period (200 replications per cell); Monte Carlo standard errors and bootstrap intervals; further benchmarks (DOTM, the M4 Comb benchmark, TimesFM-2.5, Chronos-Bolt, an all-zero forecast for intermittent demand, split-conformal intervals); the M4 official test period with OWA and multiple-comparison tests; and the Oracle ARIMA baseline made reproducible. Two conclusions changed: the robustness of TimesFM-3 is specific to that model, and its MASE advantage on intermittent demand is matched by the all-zero forecast, its advantage there lying in the predictive distribution. The study is framed as exploratory.

Version 1.2.0 (September 2026). Second round of (simulated) referee review for the Journal of Forecasting; manuscript shortened to 23 pages with a 9-page Supporting Information. All additions are post hoc and logged in DEVIATIONS.md (D-13, D-14): simple history-based benchmarks on intermittent demand, which match TimesFM-3 (its earlier pinball-loss advantage held only against Gaussian classical quantiles); the model forms chosen by AutoETS/AutoARIMA with two seasonal cycles (non-seasonal fall-backs); two newer foundation models (Chronos-2, TiRex) and a matched TimesFM-2.5 configuration; the published point forecasts of the ten best M4 submissions on the same 1,000 series (four are ahead of TimesFM-3); a cross-check of the classical methods against R's forecast package (one StatsForecast optimisation failure found); a forest plot of the pairwise effects; and a 48-step horizon, at which the robustness of TimesFM-3 disappears and every foundation model forecasts a decline on a saturated process. The split-conformal comparison was withdrawn. Downloaded M4 submissions and the raw 48-step forecasts are not archived; the code re-creates them.

Version 1.2.1 (September 2026). Final pre-submission version for the Journal of Forecasting (23 pages, Supporting Information 9 pages), approved by all authors. Restructured after an editorial review (contributions, hypotheses stated before the results, one post-hoc section, summary-of-findings table); 'scenario' replaces 'cell'. Post hoc (DEVIATIONS D-15): heavy tails and outliers combined; count-data benchmarks (iETS) for intermittent demand; 101 FRED-MD series observed after the models' documented training data, on which TimesFM-3 is statistically level with the classical methods; simultaneous intervals; a familiarity check; instance-space transfer; M4 length reweighting; six newer foundation models cited. Final numbers audit applied. Classical timings include one-off compilation and are stated as slight upper bounds. FRED-MD data and the published M4 forecasts are fetched by the code, not archived.

Version 1.2.2 (September 2026). Timing re-run on an idle machine (code/L7_timing_warmup.py): after a warm-up the classical timings differ from the earlier ones by less than 10%, and TimesFM-3 takes 24.9 ms per series on the GPU and 47.1 ms on the CPU. Section 7.3 of the manuscript reports these figures; no other change. Approved by all authors.

notes: The per-series result files are large by design: they exist so that a referee can check any number in the paper without re-running the simulation, and so that a later study can re-analyse the same forecasts under a different metric. That matters here in particular, because the paper's headline result on intermittent demand REVERSES between absolute-error and squared-error metrics, and the raw forecasts are what let anyone verify that.
